description: We are an ambitious team from the MINT-Exzellenzgymnasium, sponsored by Schüler forschungszentrum building an interactive, physics- and data-driven game in Unreal Engine for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Using a strong tech stack of Python, C++ and  Blender for 3D assets, we are turning complex NASA data and space mechanics into a highly functional, playable prototype.
summary:
Sol Zero is a first-person Mars survival game for kids ages 7 to 12, built in Unreal Engine. The player is the first human to land on Mars. A base, solar panels and a fission reactor are already waiting, but the player has to make them work. They drill for water, grow food, clean dust off the solar panels and survive solar storms. With only one reactor, they must also decide where to spend limited energy.

For the “Junior astronaut mission trainer” challenge, Sol Zero turns real NASA research into gameplay. Kids learn through play how subsurface ice, Kilopower-style fission power, MOXIE oxygen production and Mars dust and radiation shape life on another planet.

It matters because today’s kids are the generation that may actually go to Mars. Many space games lean on fantasy, while NASA’s real science stays in papers that children don’t read. Sol Zero closes that gap and teaches resource management and problem-solving along the way.
details:
What it does and how it works
Sol Zero is a first-person Mars survival game for kids ages 7 to 12. The player lands as the first human on Mars, and a base, solar panels and a fission reactor are already there. To survive, the player drills for water, grows food, makes oxygen, cleans dust off the solar panels and gets through solar storms. The main mechanic is survival. After an accident, with only one fission reactor, the player must decide where to spend limited energy: life support, water drilling, the greenhouse or the panel cleaning. Each choice has a consequence.

Benefits and intended impact
Kids learn real Mars science by acting on it, not by reading about it. They learn why dust, radiation and power matter, and they practice planning and trade-offs. We want to inspire the generation that may actually go to Mars to see themselves as astronauts. We also want to show that accurate NASA research can be as exciting as fantasy.

Tools and technology

  • Unreal Engine: game engine and programming
  • Onshape: CAD for the rover and base
  • Blender: capsule, the rest of the 3D models and animations
  • Krita: hand-painted UI
  • Real NASA sources: MOXIE oxygen experiment, Kilopower and Fission Surface Power, Mars subsurface ice maps, Mars dust and solar-storm research

What is creative
Most space games use fantasy to make Mars exciting. We use NASA’s real problems (water, power, dust, radiation) as the challenge itself. Our team built the large assets by hand, including the base, rover and UI. We used AI only where time pressure forced it: some animations, the player and parts of the interior. We say so openly.

What our team considered

  • Age group: Mechanics had to be simple enough for 7-year-olds yet deep enough for 12-year-olds.
  • Accuracy: We checked the science against official NASA material instead of inventing it.
  • Scope: We had only hackathon time, so we built a focused core loop first. After the hackathon we plan more story and research.
  • Access: Judges can play without registration.
